newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Spreads widen as long yields soar.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Spreads widen as long yields soar.

text.p: For the first time in weeks, the spread between the U.S. Treasury two-year note and 30-year bond widened, as a combination of technical and fundamental factors sent longer-dated yields sharply higher.

As the market awaits Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony next week, more steepening is expected amid fears Greenspan will tell Congress wage pressures continue to build.

The long end "should give up more ground going into that," said Kevin Sluder, head trader at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "There is more downside risk than upside, so over the next week we should see more steepening.
"If we get shocking comments (from Greenspan), then we will flatten," he added.

Players said short-term yields are fairly priced to a 5.25 percent federal funds rate. Short-term yields falling much further would consitute pricing in an ease -- which is not even a remote possibility in the near term.

"The short end is nailed down because the Fed is not changing the fed funds rate, so the long end has to do most of the work" to widen or narrow spreads, said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities LLC.

The 30-year bond was down nearly one point on Thursday, pushing its yield up to 6.65 percent -- its highest point in more than a week -- from late Wednesday's 6.58 percent. With the yield on the two-year note up to 5.84 percent from 5.80 percent, the yield curve steepened on Thursday to 81 basis points from 78. The spread had edged down from nearly 90 basis points last month.
The move was not viewed as a sea-change in market thinking, analysts said. "It's a combination of a weak currency and strong data today," Levenson said.
On the surface, Thursday's move appears small. But for weeks, both short and long term rates have moved in tandem, keeping the two-year to 30-year spread around 85 basis points.

After the producer price index showed less inflationary pressure than the market expected, "we got euphoria priced into the market," said Sluder, adding that there was little room left to rally when consumer price index (CPI) confirmed a benign inflation outlook.
"We got good news in CPI but there's nowhere else to go" Sluder said, explaining the higher yields..

Meanwhile, the dollar had fallen to 122.45 yen and 1.6835 marks, from 124.50 yen and 1.6980 marks late Wednesday, which players said may be a signal to Japanese and others to sell U.S.-denominated assets.
Along with a sharp selloff in Treasuries, stock prices slid on Thursday, with the Dow Jones industrial average trading down almost 100 points heading into the close.

Thursday's economic news was the catalyst that started the day's selloff, as initial jobless claims rose a scant 1,000 in the week ended February 15 to 309,000 -- a sign that labor markets remain tight.
Meanwhile, the Philadelphia Fed's February business outlook survey showed a rise in its overall manufacturing index to 17.4 from 11.3 in January. New orders, shipments and prices also posted gains.
Making matters worse late in the session, the March bond contract broke below what traders said was a key level in 113-05 -- pushing yields up further.
"It's hard to get excited about the bond market," Levenson said.
